prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable measurements of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a clean piece of atomic-structure physics: choose the wavelength at which the light shift of the two clock levels cancels, and thousands of neutral atoms can be held tightly without perturbing the transition. Katori made that proposal and realised the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group then drove the systematic uncertainty and stability to about 1e-18 and showed the many-body, Fermi-degenerate version. The outcome is a new regime of measurement: gravitational redshift resolved across millimetres, tight limits on drifting constants, and a credible path to redefining the second. Strontium and ytterbium clocks in many national laboratories agree with each other, including over intercontinental links, so this is the reproduced, theory-and-experiment-consistent kind of result I trust. The two-name credit is natural and fair. It is also a discovery-through-invention in the best sense, because a basic quantum idea turned into an instrument that tests the foundations.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The frequency comb (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion control and ion clocks (Wineland, 2012) are both preconditions or neighbours, so the committee could read lattice clocks as a continuation rather than a new discovery. The formal redefinition of the second has not happened, so some of the payoff is still prospective. Pierre Lemonde and others who contributed to the lattice-clock programme, and the ion-clock groups, are outside the credited names. The prize would also be about a measurement tool more than about a surprise in nature, which is a sensitivity I share given my own remarks about wanting to learn something unexpected.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B004 only eighth, as a measurement advance that connects to tests of gravity, and worries about overlap with Hall and Hansch (2005) and about Ye's name appearing in other candidacies.
responses.response: I take the 2005 overlap seriously, but I read it differently. The comb was the ruler that made optical frequency counting possible. The lattice clock is a separate idea about how to hold the atoms so that Doppler, recoil and light shifts all drop out together, and it has produced a different class of result (millimetre redshift, 1e-18 comparisons). Ye's appearance in another entry is an allocation question only if that entry is also prized; with Katori and Ye as the pair, the citation is self-contained. Your point that clocks bear on gravity is, to me, a reason to value it more, not less: it is a laboratory test of relativity at a scale nobody could reach before.

responses.point: Johansson places circuit QED first as a genuinely new quantum-optical platform underlying essentially all superconducting processors, and also flags his own closeness to the groups involved.
responses.response: I agree circuit QED is a real discovery and not just an application, and I am glad the conflict is flagged. My concern is timing and attribution. The 2025 prize was for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits, so the committee would be crowning the same technological family twice in two years. The credit among Blais, Girvin, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is also not cleanly separable into three, as your own opening and Kroll's differ on exactly this point. Lattice clocks have no comparable timing or four-into-three problem, which is why I put them ahead for this year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for the prediction-then-experiment link of Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and ranks optical lattice clocks sixth while deferring to AMO colleagues.
responses.response: The prediction followed by a striking confirmation is exactly the theory-to-experiment link I value, and I agree the correlated phases are reproduced widely. My reservation is that the pairing mechanism is still debated and Yuan Cao, first author of the decisive experiments, is outside the credited names. The field is only about eight years old. Optical clocks are settled in the sense you describe: independent laboratories agree at the 1e-18 level. I am not arguing B010 is unworthy, and I list it as an alternative, but I would want the committee to be comfortable with the superconductivity question first.

responses.point: Kroll also ranks B004 first as an originality-plus-payoff measurement advance, and treats the two-name credit as clean, while noting the question of distinctness from 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: We agree on the core case. I would add that, as an atomic theorist, I find the magic-wavelength condition the part that is genuinely a discovery about atomic structure, not just engineering, since it depends on the dynamic polarizabilities of the clock states and on controlling higher-order light shifts. On your earlier prizes concern, I would ask for the citation to name the lattice and magic-wavelength concept explicitly, so the prize is not read as a general clock prize. Where we differ slightly is on B013: you rank it fifth too, but I think it is premature and the four-into-three attribution is a worse problem than for clocks.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the hexatic melting trio of Young, Halperin and Nelson first as a simple universal mechanism that is overdue, while recognising possible overlap with the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I am drawn to the elegance of a universal mechanism explaining something messy, and I defer to you on soft-matter priority. My doubt is not merit but how the committee would frame it next to the 2016 award for topological defects and phase transitions: the hexatic extension looks like the natural sequel, and I would worry the citation reads as completing that earlier prize. I would also want your confirmation that the order of melting, continuous versus weakly first-order, is settled enough for a prize motivation. That is what keeps it behind lattice clocks in my own ordering, not a lack of respect for the physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on how the citation is worded.
Whether any additional early contributor to the magic-wavelength lattice proposal should be credited; the shortlist offers only Katori and Ye.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes the timing better or whether the committee prefers to wait for it.

How the committee weighs a precision-measurement prize against the discovery of something unexpected about nature; my view is that the gravitational-redshift and constants tests carry real foundational content.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B004: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. My close collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, and with Keller's group, does not touch the optical-lattice-clock candidate, and I would flag it if an attosecond candidate were shortlisted. For alternatives, I have no documented link to the Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich group or to the twisted-bilayer-graphene group.
